children: Proxy advisory firm InGovern has said that Fortis Healthcare is being made to answer for the conduct of former promoters it parted ways with years ago as the Delhi High Court’s forensic audit into the Singh brothers’ dealings draws the listed company and its present management into its scope.

On August 31, the Delhi High Court appointed a forensic auditor in the long-running proceedings brought by Daiichi Sankyo, which holds a Singapore arbitration award against the Singh brothers, the erstwhile promoters of Fortis, in their personal capacity.

The audit is to reconstruct the movement of Fortis shares held by the brothers since May 2016. While doing so, the High clarified that the exercise is fact-finding and imposes no liability, and Fortis has confirmed that no monetary liability has been placed on it.
The Singh brothers resigned from the Fortis board in February 2018, after which an independent board took charge ahead of IHH’s investment.

Against that backdrop, InGovern argued that the burden of the audit is falling on the wrong shoulders. “Fortis under current ownership has spent a decade rebuilding governance, expanding capacity, and delivering patient care — a genuine turnaround story now overshadowed by conduct that predates this management entirely. The people who allegedly moved the money are the Singh brothers — largely silent in this round of proceedings — while the reputational and operational burden falls on the listed operating company and its current shareholders,” the proxy adviser said.

InGovern noted that SEBI had found the Singh brothers treated Fortis as a “cash cow,” siphoning around ₹400 crore from the company and driving it to the edge of insolvency, and that Fortis is itself pursuing the brothers to recover that money.
“It was the “₹4,000 crore infusion by IHH that brought the company back from the brink, preserved thousands of jobs, and restored value for retail and institutional shareholders,” it added.

The proxy adviser was careful to note that the audit is an investigative, fact-finding exercise that does not by itself establish wrongdoing or liability on the part of Fortis or its officers, and that the matter remains before the court. Its concern, it said, is that the operational and reputational cost of the audit is being borne by the company, its employees and its patients rather than by the individuals accused of the underlying conduct.

title: Fortis made to pay for former promoters’ conduct, says Ingovern
